idiom_name: single-threaded event loop with immutable state and a reducer
implementation_notes: JavaScript runs one thread for application code, so the *class* of problem STM exists to solve - two threads mutating shared state concurrently - largely does not arise. What does arise is the same hazard one event-loop tick later: an `await` between two reads, and another task's continuation has run in between. The idiomatic fix is the reducer: compute the next state as a pure function of (state, action) and publish it once, so there is no observable intermediate. If shared mutable state genuinely spans a worker boundary - SharedArrayBuffer, a Web Worker, or Node's worker_threads - then the relevant primitives are Atomics.wait/Atomics.notify over a SharedArrayBuffer plus an Int32Array view, and the pattern to build is the validate-then-act CAS loop: read the version, compute, Atomics.compareExchange the version, and on failure re-read everything and retry. Building a general STM over JavaScript's object model is not worth it: you cannot intercept property reads to build a read set, so the abstraction has no way to see the accesses it must track.
alternative: pure reducer with immutable state published once per tick; Atomics.wait / Atomics.notify over a SharedArrayBuffer when state really is shared across workers
pitfalls: Awaiting between the read and the write of a composite update, letting another task interleave exactly as a second thread would.
Mutating `state` in place inside a reducer, which defeats the immutability the pattern depends on.
Assuming single-threaded JavaScript means no races: Web Workers, SharedArrayBuffer, and any await point are all interleaving points.
Atomics on a SharedArrayBuffer that is not declared shared - postMessage copies the object and the atomics operate on a different buffer.
Using a BigInt64Array view for the CAS word while a 32-bit atomics view is also present; mixing widths over the same buffer is an easy source of torn state.
